title: Glaze pen decoration on bisqueware
subtitle: Drawing precise lines and motifs onto bisqueware using a glaze pen before the glaze firing
excerpt: A glaze pen is a fine-tipped tool pre-loaded with underglaze or glaze slip that allows you to draw directly onto bisqueware before the glaze firing. Unlike brush painting, a glaze pen gives a fine, controlled line: suitable for botanical drawings, geometric borders, and calligraphy. No specialist skill is required beyond the ability to draw the design itself.
sourceNotes: Glaze pen decoration technique documented in contemporary studio ceramics decoration practice. Underglaze pen tools are commercially available and widely used in ceramics education.

glossaryTerms.definition: First-fired clay before the glaze firing. Bisque is porous and absorbent: glaze pen lines adhere to it well.
A pigment-bearing decorating medium applied to bisque before glazing. Formulated to survive the glaze firing beneath a clear or transparent glaze.

Decoration applied over a fired glaze surface and re-fired at a lower temperature to fuse. Glaze pen decoration applied over bisque is technically an underglaze; some glaze pen products are designed for over-glaze use on already-glazed and fired surfaces.

content.text: Glaze pens come in two types. Underglaze pens are applied before the clear glaze coat and fired under it.
Overglaze
pens are applied after the glaze firing and re-fired at a lower temperature. This tutorial uses the underglaze approach. Decorate the
bisque
first, then apply a clear glaze coat on top. The fired line sits sealed under the glaze. This gives it depth and clarity that surface overglaze cannot match.
What to buy
Underglaze

pen lines look light before firing and deepen in the kiln. Blues become a deep cobalt. Greens shift slightly toward teal. Reds shift orange at cone 6 but are truer at cone 04. Always test a sample line on a spare bisque tile first. This confirms the colour under your specific clear glaze before you decorate a finished piece.
Applying the decoration

Prepare the bisque piece: clean off any dust with a dry brush. Handle the bisque as little as possible: finger oils inhibit glaze and underglaze adhesion. If the bisque has been handled, wipe with a clean, barely-damp sponge and allow to dry before penning.

Sketch the design lightly with a soft graphite pencil on the bisque surface if needed. The pencil marks burn away in the kiln: they will not show in the finished piece. Do not use ink or felt-tip markers on bisque, which can bleed.

Prime the pen according to the manufacturer's instructions: usually by shaking and pressing the nib down on a test surface until the underglaze flows. Bisqueware absorbs liquid faster than paper; the pen may feel like it runs out faster than expected. Apply with a light, consistent touch and keep the pen moving.

Draw the design onto the bisque. The line dries almost immediately as the bisque absorbs the moisture. Errors cannot be erased: work confidently rather than slowly. Practice the design on paper first.
Allow the underglaze decoration to dry fully before applying the clear glaze coat. Wipe the foot ring clear of underglaze and glaze. Fire to the manufacturer's specified cone.
What it looks like before and after firing

Underglaze pen lines look light before firing and deepen in the kiln. Blues become a deep cobalt. Greens shift slightly toward teal. Reds shift orange at cone 6 but are truer at cone 04. Always test a sample line on a spare bisque tile first. This confirms the colour under your specific clear glaze before you decorate a finished piece.
Common mistakes

Lines blur or feather after firing: underglaze bleeding under the clear glaze. This happens if the clear glaze was applied too thickly, or if the underglaze was not fully dried before glazing. Allow full drying and apply clear glaze at normal thickness.
Pen scratches rather than drawing on the bisque surface: pen nib worn or bisque too coarse. Use a fresh pen; or work on a smoother bisque body.
Colour disappears in firing: wrong temperature range for the pen used. Confirm the pen's rated cone against the kiln's firing cone before decorating.

rows.cause: Air bubble in the pen reservoir; or pen nib absorbed bisque too fast
rows.fix: Shake and re-prime the pen on a scrap of paper. Work in shorter strokes, lifting the pen and re-priming between lines.

rows.problem: Design looks too faint after firing even though it was visible on bisque
rows.cause: Clear glaze applied too thick over the underglaze; underglaze colour not strong enough
rows.fix: Apply the clear glaze at thinner than normal (the line needs to be readable through the glaze without excessive dilution). Use a pen with a higher underglaze concentration.
